items.title: Inverse function theorem, manifold form

milnor.label: §1, Inverse Function Theorem
milnor.statement: For a smooth $f : U \to \mathbb R^k$ with $U$ open in $\mathbb R^k$, Milnor states on p. 4 that if the derivative $df_x : \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R^k$ is nonsingular then $f$ carries every sufficiently small open set $U'$ about $x$ diffeomorphically onto the open set $f(U')$. He gives no proof, referring to Apostol and to Dieudonné, and warns that $f$ may fail to be injective in the large even if $df_x$ is nonsingular everywhere. The manifold version is never stated: on p. 7 he simply says that at a regular point $f$ carries a neighbourhood of $x$ in $M$ diffeomorphically onto an open subset of $N$.
milnor.note: One of the few results in the book quoted from the literature rather than proved.

lean.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be manifolds without boundary over the real or complex scalars, $x \in M$, and let $f$ be of class $C^n$ with $n \ge 1$ on a neighbourhood of $x$, with $df_x$ invertible as a continuous linear map. Then $f$ is a $C^n$ local diffeomorphism at $x$: it restricts to a $C^n$ diffeomorphism from an open $U \ni x$ onto an open $V \ni f(x)$. The model space of $M$ is assumed complete but not finite-dimensional, and equality of dimensions is replaced by invertibility of $df_x$. A second form assumes $f$ of class $C^n$ everywhere, which is Milnor's hypothesis.

diff: Milnor quotes the Euclidean case from Apostol and Dieudonné; the formal statement is proved, and it is the manifold case, which he uses from p. 7 on without stating it.
Milnor's $f$ is smooth; the formal statement allows real or complex scalars and class $C^n$ for any $n \ge 1$, the local inverse being of the same class.
Equal dimensions are replaced by invertibility of $df_x$ as a continuous linear map, and the model space of $M$ need only be complete, not finite-dimensional.
The hypothesis is that $f$ is $C^n$ on a neighbourhood of $x$, not merely at $x$: for $n = \infty$ the weaker form gives no single open set on which $f$ is $C^\infty$.

items.title: Regular points and regular values

milnor.label: §1, p. 7
milnor.statement: For a smooth $f : M \to N$ between manifolds of the same dimension, Milnor calls $x \in M$ a regular point when $df_x$ is nonsingular, and $y \in N$ a regular value when $f^{-1}(y)$ contains only regular points; otherwise $x$ is a critical point and $f(x)$ a critical value, and every $y \in N$ is one or the other according as $f^{-1}(y)$ does or does not meet the critical set. A footnote promises that the equal-dimension restriction will be dropped in §2, where (p. 10) a regular point is one at which $df_x$ is onto.
milnor.note: The two definitions, §1 by nonsingularity and §2 by surjectivity, agree exactly when $\dim M = \dim N$.

lean.statement: The formal definitions take the §2 form from the start: $x$ is a regular point when $df_x : TM_x \to TN_{f(x)}$ is surjective and a critical point otherwise; $y$ is a regular value when every $x$ with $f(x) = y$ is a regular point, and a critical value when it is the image of a critical point. No relation between the dimensions enters. That the two definitions agree is a separate statement, proved when both model spaces are finite-dimensional of the same rank; and a point outside the image of $f$ is recorded as a regular value.

diff: The formal definition of a regular point is Milnor's §2 one, used from §1 onward, so no equality of dimensions is built into the definition.
The equivalence with Milnor's §1 definition is a theorem, needing both model spaces finite-dimensional of equal rank; it is what turns surjectivity back into invertibility.
That a point outside the image of $f$ is vacuously a regular value is stated on its own, because the counting argument of p. 9 applies to such points.

items.title: A regular fibre over a compact manifold is finite

milnor.label: §1, p. 8
milnor.statement: Milnor observes, in italics and without a label, that if $M$ is compact and $y \in N$ is a regular value then $f^{-1}(y)$ is a finite set, possibly empty. His reason is that $f^{-1}(y)$ is a closed subset of the compact $M$, hence compact, and discrete because $f$ is injective near each of its points.
milnor.note: He treats it as an immediate consequence of the inverse function theorem, in one sentence of proof.

lean.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be manifolds without boundary over the real or complex scalars, modelled on finite-dimensional spaces of equal dimension, with $M$ compact and points of $N$ closed, and let $f$ be of class $C^n$ for some $n \ge 1$. If $y$ is a regular value of $f$ then $f^{-1}(y)$ is finite. The hypothesis on $N$ is exactly the $T_1$ axiom, needed so that $f^{-1}(y)$ is closed.

diff: The formal statement names the hypothesis that points of $N$ are closed; Milnor's manifolds lie in Euclidean space, so this is automatic for him and he uses it silently.
Milnor's $f$ is smooth; the formal statement needs only class $C^n$ for some $n \ge 1$, and allows complex as well as real scalars.
Neither statement assumes $M$ or $N$ connected, nonempty, or second countable.

items.title: Local constancy of the fibre count

milnor.label: §1, p. 8
milnor.statement: For $f : M \to N$ with $M$ compact and $y$ a regular value, Milnor writes $\#f^{-1}(y)$ for the number of preimages and says it is locally constant as a function of $y$, adding the parenthesis that $y$ is to range only over regular values. The explanation he gives is a neighbourhood $V$ of $y$ with $\#f^{-1}(y') = \#f^{-1}(y)$ for every $y' \in V$, built as the intersection of the images of disjoint neighbourhoods $U_1, \dots, U_k$ of the preimages, minus the image of the rest of $M$.
milnor.note: His bracketed construction of $V$ puts no condition on $y'$, so his own proof gives the equality at every $y'$ in $V$.

lean.statement: With $M$ compact, $M$ and $N$ Hausdorff manifolds without boundary modelled on finite-dimensional spaces of equal dimension, $f$ of class $C^n$ for some $n \ge 1$, and $y$ a regular value, there is a neighbourhood of $y$ on which $\#f^{-1}(y')$ equals $\#f^{-1}(y)$ for every point $y'$, regular or not. A companion statement adds that every such $y'$ is again a regular value, which is what Chapter 4 uses.

diff: Milnor's parenthesis restricts the argument of $\#f^{-1}$ to regular values; the formal conclusion holds for every $y'$ in the neighbourhood, which is what his construction of $V$ actually delivers.
Hausdorffness of $M$ (to separate the finitely many preimages) and of $N$ (so that the image of the complement of the $U_i$ is closed) are hypotheses here and silent in the book.
The companion statement, that the nearby $y'$ are themselves regular values, is not in the book; it is proved from the local inverses that the same argument produces.

items.title: The counting principle behind the FTA

milnor.label: §1, p. 9
milnor.statement: In the last paragraph of the proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra Milnor argues that the regular values of $f$, being the sphere minus finitely many points, form a connected set, so the locally constant function $\#f^{-1}(y)$ is constant there; since it cannot vanish identically it vanishes nowhere, and $f$ is onto. He states no theorem: the argument is written for the particular map $f : S^2 \to S^2$ coming from the polynomial.
milnor.note: Nothing in the paragraph uses polynomials or spheres beyond compactness, equal dimension and connectedness of the set of regular values.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be compact, $M$ and $N$ Hausdorff manifolds without boundary modelled on finite-dimensional spaces of equal dimension, and $f$ of class $C^n$ for some $n \ge 1$. The fibre count is constant on any preconnected set of regular values; hence if $R$ is a preconnected set of regular values meeting the image of $f$, then $R$ lies in the image. If the whole set of regular values is preconnected and meets the image, $f$ is surjective, critical values being in the image by definition.

chips: a proof step made a theorem
diff: Milnor states nothing here: the reasoning is three sentences inside the proof for $f : S^2 \to S^2$, and the formal version isolates it as a theorem about arbitrary $M$ and $N$.
The formal statement comes in a local form, for any preconnected set $R$ of regular values meeting the image, and a global form, which is the sentence Milnor uses.
The last step, that critical values are in the image by definition, is left implicit in the book and is discharged explicitly in the global form.
As in V1.3 and V1.4, $M$ and $N$ are required Hausdorff and $f$ only of class $C^n$ with $n \ge 1$.

items.title: The fundamental theorem of algebra

milnor.label: §1, The fundamental theorem of algebra
milnor.statement: Every nonconstant complex polynomial $P(z)$ has a zero. Milnor proves it by passing from the plane to the unit sphere $S^2 \subset \mathbb R^3$: stereographic projection $h_+$ from the north pole turns $P$ into a map $f : S^2 \to S^2$ fixing the north pole, which is smooth there because in the chart $h_-$ it becomes $z^n$ divided by the polynomial with conjugated and reversed coefficients. The critical points are the zeros of $P'$, finite in number, so the regular values form a connected set, and the counting argument makes $f$ onto.
milnor.note: The proof is offered as the first application of regular values, at the end of §1.

lean.statement: Every complex polynomial of positive degree has a root; for polynomials over $\mathbb C$ this is Milnor's nonconstancy hypothesis verbatim. The compact surface is the Riemann sphere $\mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}$ with the charts $z$ and $1/z$, rather than $S^2$ with stereographic projection; the two are diffeomorphic, a fact neither needed nor proved. In that presentation the map read in the chart $1/z$ at both ends is $w^n$ over the reversed polynomial, with the original coefficients and no conjugation, and $\infty$ is simply placed among the critical values instead of being shown regular.

items.title: Sard's theorem

milnor.label: §3, Theorem of Sard
milnor.statement: Let $f : U \to \mathbb R^p$ be smooth with $U$ open in $\mathbb R^n$, and let $C$ be the set of $x \in U$ at which the rank of $df_x$ is less than $p$. Then $f(C) \subseteq \mathbb R^p$ has measure zero. Milnor notes that the cases $n \le p$ are comparatively easy but gives one proof covering all of them, by induction on $n$ in three steps, the third by counting cubes.
milnor.note: He restates the theorem here, having announced it in §2 (p. 10); a footnote credits the proof to Pontryagin, simplified by assuming $f$ infinitely differentiable.

lean.statement: Let $E$ and $F$ be finite-dimensional real normed spaces, $U \subseteq E$ open, and $f$ smooth on $U$, and let $C$ be the set of points of $U$ at which $df_x$ fails to be surjective. Then $f(C)$ is null for every Haar measure on $F$, taken with its Borel sets. The two degenerate cases the book passes over are split off: if $\dim F = 0$ then $C$ is empty, and if $\dim E = 0$ and $\dim F > 0$ then $f(C)$ has at most one point.

diff: Milnor's $\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^p$ with Lebesgue measure becomes arbitrary finite-dimensional real normed spaces with an arbitrary Haar measure on the target.
The generality is forced by the proof rather than sought: the induction on $\dim E$ passes to hyperplanes of $E$, which are not literally $\mathbb R^{n-1}$.
Milnor's condition $\mathrm{rank}\,df_x < p$ appears as non-surjectivity of $df_x$, the same condition; $E$ and $F$ must lie in one universe of the type theory, a formality.
The case $\dim F = 0$ must be excluded by hand, since a Haar measure on a zero-dimensional space is a point mass and not the zero measure; $\dim E = 0$ is handled separately.

items.title: Regular values are dense in Euclidean space

milnor.label: §2, p. 10
milnor.statement: Immediately after stating Sard's theorem for a smooth $f : U \to \mathbb R^n$ with $U$ open in $\mathbb R^m$, Milnor remarks that a set of measure zero contains no nonempty open set, so the complement $\mathbb R^n \setminus f(C)$ is everywhere dense. A footnote credits the density statement to Arthur B. Brown in 1935, rediscovered by Dubovickiĭ and by Thom.
milnor.note: A remark, not a numbered result; §3 proves only the measure-zero half.

lean.statement: In the same setting as the formal Sard theorem — $E$ and $F$ finite-dimensional real normed spaces, $U \subseteq E$ open, $f$ smooth on $U$, and $C$ the set where $df_x$ is not surjective — the complement of $f(C)$ is dense in $F$. No measure appears in the statement: the proof chooses the Haar measure attached to a basis of $F$ and uses that a null set has empty interior, which is Milnor's one-line reason.

diff: Milnor's remark is about $\mathbb R^n$; the formal statement is about an arbitrary finite-dimensional real normed space $F$, the Haar measure being chosen inside the proof.
The conclusion is purely topological, so the target needs no measure structure in the statement, unlike the Sard theorem it is deduced from.

items.title: Brown's theorem: regular values are dense

milnor.label: §2, Corollary (A. B. Brown)
milnor.statement: For a smooth $f : M \to N$ from an $m$-manifold to an $n$-manifold, Milnor calls $x$ critical when $df_x : TM_x \to TN_{f(x)}$ has rank less than $n$, and calls $N \setminus f(C)$ the set of regular values. Since $M$ is covered by countably many neighbourhoods each diffeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, he concludes that the set of regular values of $f$ is everywhere dense in $N$.
milnor.note: The countable cover is asserted rather than assumed: for his manifolds, subsets of Euclidean space, it comes for free.

lean.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds without boundary, modelled on finite-dimensional real normed spaces, with $M$ second countable, and let $f : M \to N$ be smooth. Then the set of $y \in N$ all of whose preimages are regular points is dense in $N$. No separation axiom on $M$ or $N$ is needed, and $N$ carries no measure: the proof reads $f$ in countably many charts of $M$ and in one chart of $N$ meeting the given open set, and applies the Euclidean statement there.

diff: Milnor's countable cover by chart neighbourhoods becomes a hypothesis: $M$ is assumed second countable, which is automatic for the subsets of $\mathbb R^k$ he works with.
The target carries no measure; the measure lives on the model space of a chart of $N$, so the conclusion is stated purely as density of a subset of $N$.

items.title: Compact 1-manifold: even number of boundary points

milnor.label: Appendix, Theorem
milnor.statement: Milnor proves that every smooth connected 1-manifold is diffeomorphic to the circle $S^1$ or to an interval of real numbers, so that up to diffeomorphism there are exactly four connected 1-manifolds. The boundary count is nowhere stated in the Appendix: it is used in the text, on p. 14, in the form that a compact 1-manifold is a union of finitely many circles and arcs and so has an even number of boundary points, with a footnote pointing to the Appendix for the proof.
milnor.note: The proof rests on parametrization by arc length and on Lemma 1 (p. 54), that two such parametrizations overlap in at most two components, two components forcing $S^1$.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff space with a charted-space structure over a model $H$ homeomorphic to the half-line $[0,\infty)$, and let $B \subseteq M$ be a set such that every chart of the atlas sends exactly the points of $B$ in its domain to coordinate $0$. Then $B$ is finite and has an even number of points. Nothing beyond the topology is assumed: charts are homeomorphisms, there is no smooth structure, no arc length, and neither connectedness nor second countability is required.

diff: Milnor's 1-manifolds are smooth and his proof uses arc length; the formal theorem assumes only a topological 1-manifold with boundary, which is all the book's applications need.

The classification is not used here, and this proof does not state it: what it gives is that the component of a boundary point is the image of an arc whose coordinate interval is closed, and the circle case never arises, the parametrization being always started at a boundary point. The classification itself is now proved, in the smooth setting (V.A2), and the even count derived from it a second time (V.A3); this topological theorem is left untouched and, through V.A′, is still what Chapters 2 and 4 cite.
The boundary is given as a set $B$, with the hypothesis that every chart of the atlas, not only the chart at a given point, sends exactly the points of $B$ to coordinate $0$.
Compactness and Hausdorffness are used explicitly: the first for finiteness of $B$ and for a finite cover by chart arcs, the second to identify limits in the overlap lemma.

items.title: Even boundary count for Chapter 2's manifolds

milnor.label: §2, p. 14
milnor.statement: In the proof of Lemma 5 Milnor needs that $f^{-1}(y)$, a compact 1-manifold whose boundary is its intersection with $\partial X$, has an even number of boundary points, and gets this from the classification: such a manifold is a union of finitely many circles and arcs. A footnote refers to the Appendix for the proof. The manifolds he applies it to are the level sets produced by his Lemma 4 inside a manifold with boundary.
milnor.note: He never isolates the parity statement as a lemma; it recurs in the homotopy lemma of §4, in Lemma 1 of §5, and in §6.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a Hausdorff smooth manifold over any model with corners, its model space an arbitrary real normed space, and let $X \subseteq M$ be a compact half-slice submanifold with boundary $B \subseteq X$ modelled on the half-space over a space $Z$ with a single point — that is, a compact 1-manifold with boundary in the sense of Chapter 2. Then $B$ is finite and has an even number of points. It is deduced from the topological theorem by checking that the charted-space structure that $X$ inherits sends the points of $B$ to coordinate $0$ in every chart.

diff: Only $X$ is assumed compact and $M$ merely Hausdorff, and the model space of $M$ is an arbitrary real normed space, not required finite-dimensional or boundaryless.
Being a 1-manifold is expressed by the half-space model $\mathbb R \times Z$ having $Z$ a single point; the smooth structure of $X$ is then discarded and the topological theorem applied.

As in the topological form, this proof does not go through the classification Milnor proves: it gives only the parity of the boundary count, which is the sole consequence the book uses. The classification is proved separately (V.A2) and yields the same count a second time, with each component identified and the pairing named (V.A3); this theorem is untouched and is the one Chapters 2 and 4 cite.

items.title: Appendix Lemma 1: the overlap of two arcs, and the affine transition

milnor.label: Appendix, Lemma 1
milnor.statement: Milnor's one lemma of the Appendix (p. 54). Let $f : I \to M$ and $g : J \to M$ be parametrizations by arc length of a smooth 1-manifold $M \subseteq \mathbb R^k$ — diffeomorphisms onto open subsets whose velocity has Euclidean length $1$. Then $f(I) \cap g(J)$ has at most two connected components; if it has one, $f$ extends to a parametrization by arc length of $f(I) \cup g(J)$; and if it has two, $M$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1$. His proof studies the graph $\Gamma = \{(s, t) : f(s) = g(t)\}$: differentiating $g(\tau(s)) = f(s)$ for $\tau = g^{-1} \circ f$ gives $|\tau'| = 1$, so $\tau'$ is continuous with values $\pm 1$ and constant on each component, $\Gamma$ is a union of segments of slope $\pm 1$ running from edge to edge of the rectangle $I \times J$, and the four surviving pictures give the four cases.
milnor.note: He states the lemma only for arc-length parametrizations, and says so: a merely monotone transition would leave the constant and the shape of the reparametrization free.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a Hausdorff topological space charted on $H$, with $I : \mathrm{ModelWithCorners}\ \mathbb R\ E\ H$ over an arbitrary real normed space $E$; let $L$ be a *length element*, a density indexed not by charts but by local real parameters, so that it can be read along a chart and along an arc with no layer between; and let $A$, $A'$ be $C^\infty$ arcs of unit speed for $L$ — homeomorphisms from open subsets of $M$ onto bounded intervals of $\mathbb R$, smooth in both directions, whose coordinate advances at unit rate. Write $S$ for the overlap, the set of $A$-parameters whose point lies in $A'$ as well, and take the components of $S$ to be its maximal subintervals. Then: on each component the transition $s \mapsto A'(A^{-1}(s))$ is $s \mapsto \varepsilon s + k$ with $\varepsilon = \pm 1$; $S$ has at most two components; and two distinct components reach *opposite* ends of $A$'s interval, one running down to its infimum while the other runs up to its supremum. There is no dimension hypothesis, no manifold instance, no compactness and no boundarylessness: only Hausdorffness, which the overlap API needs to identify two limits. The second and third clauses use no smoothness whatever. The extension clause is separate and strong: the glued arc is again a smooth arc of unit speed, its source is the union of the two sources, and its coordinate *equals* the old one on the whole of the old source.

chips: topological half: no smoothness at all
the circle case counted, not excluded
diff: Milnor's $M$ is a smooth 1-manifold in a Euclidean space and his parametrizations are by Euclidean arc length. The formal statement asks only that $M$ be Hausdorff and charted on a model with corners over an arbitrary real normed space, with unit speed taken against a length element; it carries no dimension hypothesis, no manifold instance, no compactness and no boundarylessness, and it holds for a model whose range is a compact interval, which is a one-manifold *with corners*.

The lemma splits, and only one half needs unit speed. That the overlap has at most two components, and that two components reach opposite ends, hold for arcs that are merely homeomorphisms from open subsets of a Hausdorff space onto bounded intervals — no smoothness and no arc length anywhere. What genuinely needs unit speed is the affine form $s \mapsto \pm s + k$ of the transition, which comes in one line from the cocycle rule of the length element: read in a unit-speed parameter the density is $1$, so $1 = 1 \cdot |\tau'|$, and a continuous nowhere-zero $\tau'$ cannot change sign on a component.

The two-component case is **counted, not excluded**. The topological Appendix (V.A) avoids it by normalizing the first arc to start at a boundary point, which rules out the circle by fiat; here there is no hypothesis on where either arc starts, and the case that forces the circle appears as one of the alternatives. The device the earlier file lacked is the *inner* component, the one both of whose ends are interior to the first arc's interval: it runs off both ends of the other arc at once, so the transition carries it onto that arc's whole interval, and injectivity then makes it the only component. Two byproducts: the inner case is exactly the case where one arc sits inside the other, and an inner component forces the other arc to contain no boundary point at all.

Milnor's normalization turns out to have been doing nothing essential, and his third clause — two components force $S^1$ — is not proved here as a statement about $M$; it is the two-component alternative, and the circle is identified in V.A2 by a different route, through unit-speed curves of the whole line.

The extension clause is strong in a way the topological theorem cannot be. Because the transition is $s \mapsto +s + k$ with the constant pinned down from either side, the old parameter *is* the new parameter on the old source, so the glued arc genuinely extends the first rather than merely containing its image up to reparametrization; the topological theorem's conclusion is an existential that forgets the witness's coordinate, from which the transition could be recovered only as an increasing homeomorphism fixing $0$ — it could be $s \mapsto s^2$. About seventy-five lines of the topological proof then *disappear*: both one-sided limit computations at the junction and the trichotomy proofs of continuity there, because with unit-speed arcs the two branches are the same affine function on the whole overlap and there is no seam to be continuous at.

items.title: The classification of one-manifolds: Milnor's Appendix theorem

milnor.label: Appendix, Theorem
milnor.statement: Every smooth connected 1-manifold, with or without boundary, is diffeomorphic to the circle $S^1$ or to an interval of real numbers — open, closed or half-open, bounded or not — so that up to diffeomorphism there are exactly four of them. Milnor proves it by taking a maximal parametrization by arc length, Lemma 1 supplying the overlap picture at each step; the reduction of an arbitrary interval to a normal form he leaves to a parenthesis, an affine map for a bounded interval and $t \mapsto \tanh t$ for an unbounded one; and the distinctness of the four he asserts without proof. No countability hypothesis is stated, his manifolds being subsets of $\mathbb R^k$.
milnor.note: Chapters 2, 4, 5 and 6 quote only the consequence, the even boundary count, and the footnote on p. 14 points here for the proof.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a real normed space with $\dim E = 1$, let $I : \mathrm{ModelWithCorners}\ \mathbb R\ E\ H$, and let $M$ be a topological space charted on $H$ which is Hausdorff, $\sigma$-compact, connected — hence nonempty — and a $C^\infty$ manifold over $I$. Then $M$ is $C^\infty$-diffeomorphic to the circle, to $[0, 1]$, to $[0, \infty)$ or to $\mathbb R$, each with its own model with corners, and to **exactly one** of them. A sharper form keys the four alternatives to two invariants: compact with empty boundary gives the circle, compact with a boundary point $[0, 1]$, non-compact with a boundary point $[0, \infty)$, non-compact with empty boundary $\mathbb R$. Exclusivity is proved, all six pairs: compactness settles four of them, and the number of boundary points — a diffeomorphism invariant, because a diffeomorphism carries boundary onto boundary — has the values $0$, $2$, $1$, $0$ and settles the remaining one in each compactness class. The boundary is Mathlib's, and no compatibility hypothesis on the charts is assumed: the chart-independence of boundary points is proved. Nothing is assumed about the boundary, about orientability or about second countability. Nine stages and some nine thousand three hundred lines: the one-dimensional setup, with the model classified into the line, a closed half-line and a compact interval, the last a one-manifold with corners kept alive throughout; smooth arcs and their transitions; the length element, which is where Hausdorffness and $\sigma$-compactness are spent, and unit-speed arcs; the affine transition and the extension theorem (V.A1); and the four cases — the compact one with boundary by exhausting a component by arcs, the circle by a unit-speed *curve* of the whole line with a propagation lemma in place of an exhaustion, and the two non-compact ones by explicit parametrizations of the six shapes of open interval and half-line, with no inverse function theorem anywhere.

chips: exactly one: all six exclusions proved
the long line is the counterexample
diff: Milnor states no countability hypothesis and the theorem is **false** without one: the long line — two copies of the closed long ray $\omega_1 \times [0, 1)$ glued along their least elements — is a connected Hausdorff smooth one-manifold without boundary diffeomorphic to none of the four, not being second countable. So the formal statement assumes $\sigma$-compactness, which Milnor has for free, his manifolds sitting in $\mathbb R^k$, and which he uses silently: the Euclidean metric he restricts to $M$ is a Riemannian metric, and a manifold carrying one is metrizable. It is spent in exactly one place in the whole development, the existence of the length element, and only the two non-compact cases need it; in the compact cases compact plus Hausdorff plus a finite-dimensional model already gives second countability.

"Exactly four" is asserted in the book and proved here. All six exclusions are theorems: four by compactness, two by the number of boundary points, which is a diffeomorphism invariant because a diffeomorphism carries the boundary onto the boundary. The boundary of the model half-line had to be computed by hand, Mathlib having no half-line manifold; $[0, \infty)$ was given its structure here, as a one-chart manifold with boundary whose chart is a homeomorphism onto the whole model half-space.

Milnor's "an interval of real numbers" becomes the three normal forms $[0, 1]$, $[0, \infty)$ and $\mathbb R$, which is his own parenthesis carried out, and each model carries its own model with corners. Hausdorffness is assumed rather than inherited from an ambient $\mathbb R^k$, and the model space is an arbitrary real normed space of dimension one rather than $\mathbb R$ itself.

Where the design pass was wrong, and this is the substantive correction of the programme: the exhaustion of a manifold by arcs has no boundaryless analogue. Every arc of a boundaryless manifold has an *open* interval for its target, while the extension theorem needs the first arc's target to be half-open, that is, to start at a boundary point. The circle is proved instead with unit-speed *curves* of the whole line — maps agreeing near each time with the arc-length parametrization of some arc — whose engine is a propagation lemma, that two such curves agreeing near one time agree on the whole interval, proved by a connectedness argument run in the parameter of one arc rather than in the time, because the set of times of local agreement need not be closed, and the obstruction is exactly that an overlap can have two components.

Three bridges had to be built which the book does not need. The connected components of a smooth one-manifold are **open**, hence manifolds in their own right, which is what lets a theorem about connected manifolds reach a disconnected one, and is the piece the design pass never mentions. The boundary of the half-line model is a single point. And the boundary count for a possibly disconnected compact one-manifold is proved from scratch, its *finiteness* being the harder half, because V.A wants a compatibility hypothesis available only when the model range is a half-line.

A byproduct closes a hypothesis of V.A. For a smooth one-manifold whose model range is a half-line, Mathlib's boundary satisfies the compatibility condition that the topological theorem has to assume — every chart of the atlas, not only the chart at a point, sends exactly the boundary points to coordinate $0$ — with no side condition at all, and $C^1$ suffices. So V.A applies to smooth one-manifolds unconditionally.

items.title: The even boundary count, derived from the classification

milnor.label: Appendix, Theorem, last clause
milnor.statement: The last sentence of the Appendix theorem: a compact 1-manifold with boundary has an even number of boundary points. Milnor derives it from the classification — a compact manifold has finitely many components, since the components are open and form a cover with no proper subcover, and each is a circle with no boundary points or a closed interval with two. This is the only consequence of the Appendix the book uses: it is quoted on p. 14 in the proof of Lemma 5, again in the homotopy lemma of §4, in Lemma 1 of §5 and in §6, each time with a footnote pointing to the Appendix.
milnor.note: The pairing behind the parity is the two ends of one arc; Milnor leaves it in the picture and counts components instead.

lean.statement: The hypotheses of V.A′, and four conclusions read off from the classification. Let $M$ be a Hausdorff $C^\infty$ manifold over any model with corners, its model space an arbitrary real normed space; let $Z$ be a normed space with a single point; and let $X \subseteq M$ be a compact half-slice submanifold with boundary $B \subseteq X$ — that is, a compact 1-manifold with boundary in the sense of Chapter 2. Then every connected component of $X$, which is open and so a manifold in its own right, is $C^\infty$-diffeomorphic to the circle or to $[0, 1]$. The components meeting $B$ are *exactly* the ones diffeomorphic to $[0, 1]$, and the ones missing $B$ exactly the circles, both stated as equivalences. Each component that meets $B$ meets it in exactly two points. And every boundary point $p$ has exactly one partner: a boundary point $p' \ne p$ with $B \cap (\text{component of } p) = \{p, p'\}$, which is the pairing, realised by the two ends of one arc-length parametrization of that component. Hence $B$ is finite with an even number of points — the conclusion of V.A′, with a different proof: the old one counts a fixed-point-free involution built from the topological Appendix's arc extension, this one runs the classification on each component. V.A′ is left in place, is still what Chapters 2 and 4 cite, and is not used here; the only thing borrowed from the topological file is the combinatorial lemma that a fixed-point-free involution of a finite set has even cardinality.

chips: each interval gives exactly two points
the pairing: the two ends of one arc
diff: The conclusion is V.A′'s and the proof is the book's, where V.A′ argues by parity alone: the components are identified and counted, rather than an involution being exhibited on the boundary of a topological manifold. Both theorems stand, V.A′ is what Chapters 2 and 4 cite, and this row uses nothing of it beyond the combinatorics of a fixed-point-free involution.

More is proved than the book states. Milnor says a compact one-manifold is a union of finitely many circles and arcs; the formal statement says which components are which, by an equivalence in each direction — a component meets the boundary exactly when it is diffeomorphic to $[0, 1]$, and misses it exactly when it is a circle — gives each component of the second kind exactly two boundary points, and names the partner of each boundary point, which is the pairing the parity comes from.

Finiteness of the boundary is the harder half for a possibly disconnected compact one-manifold, and it could not be taken over from V.A: that theorem assumes the chart compatibility condition, which is available only when the model range is a half-line. It is proved here for the abstract manifold first and then transported.

Hypotheses as in V.A′ and no more: only $X$ is compact, $M$ is merely Hausdorff, its model space is an arbitrary real normed space, and being a one-manifold is expressed by the half-space model $\mathbb R \times Z$ with $Z$ a single point. Unlike V.A′, the smooth structure of $X$ is not discarded — it is what the classification runs on — and $\sigma$-compactness is free, $X$ being compact.

That the components of a one-manifold are open, hence manifolds in their own right, is what lets a theorem about connected manifolds reach a disconnected one. It needs only that the model space is one-dimensional: every point lies in the source of an arc, and the source of an arc is preconnected. No compactness, no Hausdorffness and no length element.

items.title: Connected one-manifolds are orientable

milnor.label: Appendix
milnor.statement: The book never states this and never needs it. Orientability as a property of a manifold is nowhere defined (V7.18), and for one-manifolds the question does not arise: Milnor's one-manifolds are the level sets $f^{-1}(y)$ in a Euclidean space, where a tangent line is a line in one fixed $\mathbb R^k$, and the signs §5 attaches to the two ends of an arc are ambient, read off from the ambient orientation rather than from an orientation of the arc. The classification of the Appendix would make the statement immediate, the circle and every interval being orientable, but Milnor draws no such conclusion, having no use for one: his remark of p. 50 restricts itself to a non-orientable $M$ and says nothing about why such an $M$ cannot be one-dimensional.
milnor.note: This row exists to remove a hypothesis, not to record a result of the book: it is what makes $2 \le m$ derivable in V7.26.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $I : \mathrm{ModelWithCorners}\ \mathbb R\ E\ H$ with $I$ **boundaryless**, and $M$ a Hausdorff, $\sigma$-compact, connected $C^\infty$ manifold charted on $H$. If $\dim E = 1$ then $M$ is orientable in the sense of V7.18. The classification (V.A2) makes $M$ diffeomorphic to the circle if it is compact and to $\mathbb R$ if it is not — the two interval models are excluded because the model is boundaryless, so the boundary of $M$ is empty — and orientability travels back along the diffeomorphism. Hence, with $\dim E = m$: a connected non-orientable $M$ has $2 \le m$, dimension $0$ being orientable because in dimension $0$ every linear map preserves every orientation, the only tuple to test being the empty one, and dimension $1$ by the previous statement. The same in the vocabulary of Chapters 7 and 8 — a compact connected non-orientable slice submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ charted on $\mathbb R^m$ has $2 \le m$ — where every hypothesis comes free: $M$ is Hausdorff as a subspace of a metric space, $\sigma$-compact because compact, and its model is boundaryless, so its boundary is empty. On the way: the pullback of an orientation along an invertible linear map and its uniqueness, a space of dimension $n$ having exactly two orientations; the transport of an orientation along any smooth map of manifolds of the same dimension whose derivative is everywhere invertible, hence in particular along a diffeomorphism; and all four models of the classification oriented. The file sits in Chapter 7, where the statement is used.

chips: the book has no use for the statement
boundaryless model, and only the source
diff: No counterpart in the book, and none is wanted there: Milnor's one-manifolds arise as level sets in a Euclidean space and carry no orientation of their own, orientability as a property of a manifold being undefined in the book (V7.18). The row is here to remove a hypothesis, and V7.26 is the only thing that uses it.

Transport of an orientation is proved along any smooth map between manifolds of the same dimension whose derivative is everywhere invertible: neither injectivity, nor surjectivity, nor being a local diffeomorphism is needed. It assumes boundarylessness of the **source** only, the target being allowed a boundary, and that single restriction is why the row is stated for boundaryless models — a chart target of the source has to be open in the model space for the map read in charts to have a genuine derivative there, continuous in the point. Transport *into* a manifold whose model has a boundary is not proved, is not needed, and is where the file stops.

All four models of the classification are oriented, and one of them is not free. Mathlib's manifold structure on $[0, 1]$ has **two** charts, $z \mapsto z$ on $[0, 1)$ and $z \mapsto 1 - z$ on $(0, 1]$, whose transition reverses orientation, so a constant family is not an orientation there and the orientation has to flip at the right endpoint; that one transition derivative is computed by factoring the chart at $1$ through the chart at an interior point and the reflection of the model space. The circle was oriented not through its own charts but through the unit circle $S^1 \subseteq \mathbb R^2$, which Chapter 8 orients as the boundary of the disk, the classification supplying the diffeomorphism; that is shorter than either direct route, the sphere being oriented already.

What the row buys is exactly the deletion of the dimension hypothesis from V7.26: non-orientability of a connected manifold now *implies* $2 \le m$, so the hypothesis the punctured stage needs (V7.22) is derived rather than assumed. Nothing else in the project depends on it.

items.title: Slice submanifolds of an abstract manifold

milnor.label: §2, p. 11
milnor.statement: The book has no notion of submanifold, because a manifold is by definition a subset of $\mathbb R^k$ that is locally diffeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$. In the proof of Lemma 1 Milnor produces a diffeomorphism $F$ of a neighbourhood of $x$ onto an open set under which $f^{-1}(y)$ becomes a coordinate hyperplane, and concludes at once that $f^{-1}(y)$ is a smooth manifold.
milnor.note: Being a manifold is a property of a subset of $\mathbb R^k$ for him, so no structure ever has to be built.

lean.statement: A slice chart for $S \subseteq M$ is a diffeomorphism $\varphi$ of an open set $U \subseteq M$ onto an open subset of $Z \times W$ with $p \in S \iff \varphi(p) \in Z \times \{0\}$ for $p \in U$; $S$ is a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$ when every point of $S$ lies in such a $U$. The formal statement is that such an $S$, with the subspace topology and the charts $p \mapsto \mathrm{pr}_Z \varphi(p)$ induced by all its slice charts, is a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on $Z$, and that the inclusion $S \to M$ is smooth. Nothing is assumed finite-dimensional: $Z$ and $W$ are arbitrary real normed spaces and the ambient $M$ may itself have boundary.

chips: dimension carried by a model space $Z$
diff: For a subset of $\mathbb R^k$ the straightening chart of Lemma 1 already is the definition of a manifold, so Milnor's proof ends there; for an abstract $M$ the atlas has to be built.
The definition takes exactly what Milnor's proof produces, a subset covered by straightening diffeomorphisms, and every later "is a manifold" in the formal text reduces to exhibiting such charts.
Milnor's dimension $m - n$ becomes a hypothesis on the model space $Z$, and the atlas consists of the charts induced by all slice charts, not only the chosen ones.

items.title: Lemma 1: the preimage of a regular value

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 1
milnor.statement: If $f : M \to N$ is a smooth map between manifolds of dimensions $m \ge n$ and $y \in N$ is a regular value, then $f^{-1}(y) \subseteq M$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $m - n$. The proof completes $f$ by a linear map $L : \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R^{m-n}$ nonsingular on the null space of $df_x$, inverts $F = (f, L)$ near $x$, and observes that $f^{-1}(y)$ becomes the hyperplane $y \times \mathbb R^{m-n}$.
milnor.note: That $M$ and $N$ are finite-dimensional and have no boundary is part of his definition of a manifold, so he states neither.

lean.statement: Let $M$, $N$ be $C^\infty$ manifolds without boundary modelled on finite-dimensional real spaces $E$, $F$, let $f : M \to N$ be smooth, and let $y$ be a regular value, meaning $df_x$ is surjective at every $x$ with $f(x) = y$. Let $Z$ be a finite-dimensional real space with $\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E$. Then $f^{-1}(y)$ is a slice submanifold of $M$ modelled on $Z$, hence by V2.1 a manifold of dimension $\dim M - \dim N$ with smooth inclusion. A refined form records that the slice chart at $x$ can be taken with second component $p \mapsto \psi(f(p)) - \psi(y)$, where $\psi$ is the extended chart of $N$ at $y$.

chips: dimension carried by a model space $Z$
diff: The dimension count $m - n$ is carried by a model space $Z$ with $\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E$; Milnor's hypothesis $m \ge n$ is precisely the existence of such a $Z$.
Finite-dimensionality of $E$ and $F$ and boundarylessness of both models are named, being part of Milnor's definition of a manifold rather than of his statement.
The conclusion is that $f^{-1}(y)$ is a slice submanifold in the sense of V2.1; the smooth structure and the smooth inclusion come from there.
The refined form, which names the second component of the chart, is not in the book; Lemma 3 is proved from it.

items.title: Lemma 2: the tangent space of a level set

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 2
milnor.statement: For a regular value $y$ of $f : M \to N$ and $M' = f^{-1}(y)$, the null space of $df_x : TM_x \to TN_y$ is precisely the tangent space $TM'_x \subseteq TM_x$; hence $df_x$ carries the orthogonal complement of $TM'_x$ in $TM_x$ isomorphically onto $TN_y$.
milnor.note: He proves it from the square $M' \to M \to N$: $df_x$ kills $TM'_x$ because $f$ is constant on $M'$, and a dimension count finishes both claims.

lean.statement: In the setting of V2.2, give $f^{-1}(y)$ the structure of V2.1 and let $\iota : f^{-1}(y) \to M$ be the inclusion. For $p \in f^{-1}(y)$ and $v \in T_pM$: $v$ lies in the image of $d\iota_p$ if and only if $df_p(v) = 0$. Two separate statements supply the halves: $df_p \circ d\iota_p = 0$, because $f \circ \iota$ is constant, and $d\iota_p$ is injective for any slice submanifold, because $\mathrm{pr}_Z \circ \varphi \circ \iota$ is the induced chart at $p$ and has derivative the identity there.

chips: elementwise, not an equality of spaces
diff: The tangent spaces of $M$ and of $f^{-1}(y)$ are modelled on different spaces, $E$ and $Z$, so the formal statement compares vectors instead of asserting $\operatorname{im} d\iota_p = \ker df_p$.

Milnor's second sentence, that $df_x$ maps the orthogonal complement of $TM'_x$ isomorphically onto $TN_y$, is a row of its own, V2.12: it needs an inner product on the model space, which an abstract $M$ does not carry.
The injectivity of $d\iota_p$, which Milnor gets free from $TM'_x \subseteq TM_x$, is proved for every slice submanifold and is what makes the dimension count available.

items.title: Manifolds with boundary: the definition

milnor.label: §2, Definition
milnor.statement: With $\mathbb H^m = \{x \in \mathbb R^m : x_m \ge 0\}$ and $\partial \mathbb H^m = \mathbb R^{m-1} \times 0$, a subset $X \subseteq \mathbb R^k$ is a smooth $m$-manifold with boundary if each of its points has a neighbourhood in $X$ diffeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb H^m$; $\partial X$ is the set of points corresponding to $\partial \mathbb H^m$ under such a diffeomorphism. He then records that $\partial X$ is well defined and is a smooth $(m-1)$-manifold, that $X - \partial X$ is an $m$-manifold, and that $TX_x$ is $m$-dimensional even at a boundary point.
milnor.note: He calls the well-definedness of $\partial X$ "not hard to show" and gives no proof.

lean.statement: The half-space is $H(Z) = \{(t,z) \in \mathbb R \times Z : t \ge 0\}$, made into a model with corners whose image has interior $\{t > 0\}$ and frontier $\{t = 0\}$. For subsets $X$, $B$ of an ambient manifold $M$, a half-slice chart is a diffeomorphism $\Phi$ of an open $U \subseteq M$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R \times Z$ with $p \in X \iff \Phi_1(p) \ge 0$ and $p \in B \iff \Phi_1(p) = 0$ for all $p \in U$, and $X$ is a half-slice submanifold with boundary $B$ when every point of $X$ lies in such a $U$. The formal statement is that such an $X$ is a smooth manifold modelled on $H(Z)$, that its boundary in Mathlib's sense is exactly $X \cap B$, and that the inclusion $X \to M$ is smooth.

diff: Milnor reads $\partial X$ off the charts and then remarks that it is well defined; the formal definition prescribes $B$ in advance and demands that every chart send exactly $B$ to $\{t = 0\}$.
So the invariance argument behind the well-definedness is never carried out; every manifold with boundary in the formal text is built with charts respecting a given $B$, which suffices downstream.
The distinguished coordinate is written first, $\{t \ge 0\} \subseteq \mathbb R \times Z$, where Milnor writes it last in $\mathbb H^m$.
$X$ is always a subset of an ambient manifold $M$, never an abstract manifold with boundary standing on its own; $M$ itself is allowed to have boundary.

items.title: Lemma 3: the region where $g \ge 0$

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 3
milnor.statement: Let $M$ be a manifold without boundary and $g : M \to \mathbb R$ a smooth function with $0$ as a regular value. Then the set of $x \in M$ with $g(x) \ge 0$ is a smooth manifold with boundary equal to $g^{-1}(0)$.
milnor.note: He gives no proof, saying only that it is just like the proof of Lemma 1.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real space $E$, let $Z$ be a finite-dimensional real space with $\dim Z + 1 = \dim E$, and let $g : M \to \mathbb R$ be smooth with $0$ a regular value. Then $\{g \ge 0\}$ is a half-slice submanifold over $Z$ with boundary $\{g = 0\}$, hence by V2.4 a manifold with boundary modelled on the half-space over $Z$.

chips: dimension carried by a model space $Z$
diff: The dimension of the boundary is carried by a model space $Z$ with $\dim Z + 1 = \dim E$, which in particular forces $\dim M \ge 1$; Milnor leaves the count implicit.
The conclusion is stated with the half-slice charts of V2.4, with $B = \{g = 0\}$ prescribed in advance rather than read off the charts.
Milnor's "just like the proof of Lemma 1" is made literal: at a boundary point the slice chart of V2.2 for $g$ has second component $g$, and swapping the factors puts $g$ first.
Regularity of $0$ is used only where $g(x) = 0$; at points with $g(x) > 0$ any chart of $M$, straightened by a linear isomorphism and translated, is a half-slice chart.

items.title: Lemma 4: level sets in a manifold with boundary

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 4
milnor.statement: Let $f : X \to N$ be smooth from an $m$-manifold with boundary to an $n$-manifold, with $m > n$. If $y \in N$ is a regular value both of $f$ and of the restriction $f|_{\partial X}$, then $f^{-1}(y) \subseteq X$ is a smooth $(m-n)$-manifold with boundary, and $\partial(f^{-1}(y))$ is exactly $f^{-1}(y) \cap \partial X$.
milnor.note: In the local model $f : \mathbb H^m \to \mathbb R^n$ he uses the regularity of $f|_{\partial \mathbb H^m}$ only to know that the null space of $df_x$ is not contained in $\mathbb R^{m-1} \times 0$.

lean.statement: Let $M$, $N$ be manifolds without boundary modelled on finite-dimensional $E$, $F$; let $Z$, $Z'$ be finite-dimensional with $\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E$ and $\dim Z' + 1 = \dim Z$; let $f : M \to N$ be smooth with $y$ a regular value of $f$ on all of $M$, and $g : M \to \mathbb R$ smooth. Assume that at every $x$ with $f(x) = y$ and $g(x) = 0$ there is a $v \in T_xM$ with $df_x(v) = 0$ and $dg_x(v) \ne 0$. Then, inside the manifold $f^{-1}(y)$ of V2.2, the set $\{g \ge 0\}$ is a half-slice submanifold over $Z'$ with boundary $\{g = 0\}$: that is, $f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g \ge 0\}$ is a manifold with boundary $f^{-1}(y) \cap \{g = 0\}$. No regularity of $0$ for $g$ is assumed anywhere.

diff: Milnor's $X$ is an arbitrary $m$-manifold with boundary; the formal $X$ is $\{g \ge 0\}$ inside a boundaryless $M$ on which $f$ is defined, which covers every later use but not his statement.
His hypothesis that $y$ is regular for $f|_{\partial X}$ becomes the transversality condition $df_x(v) = 0$, $dg_x(v) \ne 0$, which is what his proof extracts from it.
$y$ must be a regular value of $f$ on all of $M$, not only on $X$ as in the book; this holds in every application in the formal text.
Milnor's $m > n$ is the existence of $Z'$ with $\dim Z' + 1 = \dim Z$; unlike Lemma 3 this statement needs no regular value of $g$, since transversality already forces $dg_x \ne 0$ where it matters.

items.title: The unit disk, with boundary the sphere

milnor.label: §2, Example
milnor.statement: The unit disk $\mathbb D^m$, consisting of the $x \in \mathbb R^m$ with $1 - \sum x_i^2 \ge 0$, is a smooth manifold with boundary equal to $S^{m-1}$.
milnor.note: It is offered as the example produced by Lemma 3, with no verification of the regular value.

lean.statement: For a finite-dimensional real inner product space $E$ and a finite-dimensional $Z$ with $\dim Z + 1 = \dim E$, the closed unit ball of $E$ is a half-slice submanifold over $Z$ with boundary the unit sphere. The case recorded is that for every $m \ge 0$ the closed unit ball of $\mathbb R^{m+1}$ is a manifold with boundary $S^m$, modelled on the half-space over $\mathbb R^m$. Both are Lemma 3 for $g(x) = 1 - \|x\|^2$, whose derivative $v \mapsto -2\langle x, v\rangle$ is shown to be surjective wherever $\|x\| = 1$.

diff: The ambient space is written $\mathbb R^{m+1}$ with $m \ge 0$: the half-slice model needs a factor $\mathbb R$, so the statement would fail for the point $\mathbb D^0 \subseteq \mathbb R^0$.
The ball is taken in an arbitrary finite-dimensional real inner product space, and the model space $Z$ for the boundary is named; Milnor's $\mathbb D^m$ is the case $Z = \mathbb R^{m-1}$.
That $0$ is a regular value of $1 - \|x\|^2$ is proved, by exhibiting $v = -\tfrac t2 x$ with $dg_x(v) = t$ on the sphere, where Milnor simply invokes Lemma 3.

items.title: Corestriction to a submanifold

milnor.label: §2, p. 13
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement: for subsets of $\mathbb R^k$, a smooth map with values in $S$ is a smooth map into $S$ by definition, so the question never arises. Milnor uses the fact silently in Lemma 5, where a map $f : X \to \partial X$ is treated as a map into the manifold $\partial X$ so that a regular value of it may be chosen.

lean.statement: Let $S$ be a slice submanifold of $M$ in the sense of V2.1, let $M'$ be a $C^\infty$ manifold, and let $F : M' \to M$ be smooth with $F(x) \in S$ for every $x$. Then $F$ is smooth as a map $M' \to S$. Read in the chart of $S$ at $F(x)$ induced by a slice chart $\varphi$, the map is $\mathrm{pr}_Z \circ \varphi \circ F$, a composite of smooth maps.

diff: Smoothness of a map into $S \subseteq \mathbb R^k$ means smoothness into $\mathbb R^k$ for Milnor, so corestriction is invisible; for an abstract $S$ with a constructed atlas it has to be proved.
The formal statement requires the values to lie in $S$ at every point of $M'$, and is used in V2.10 to turn the retraction of the ball into a map into the sphere.

items.title: Lemma 6: the retraction formula, verified

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 6
milnor.statement: In the proof of Lemma 6 Milnor writes the retraction explicitly: for a smooth $g : \mathbb D^n \to \mathbb D^n$ without fixed points, $f(x) = x + tu$ with $u = (x - g(x))/\|x - g(x)\|$ and $t = -x \cdot u + \sqrt{1 - x \cdot x + (x \cdot u)^2}$, the expression under the square root being strictly positive, and asserts that $f$ is a smooth map $\mathbb D^n \to S^{n-1}$ with $f(x) = x$ for $x \in S^{n-1}$.
milnor.note: He calls this an explicit computation and leaves the verification to the reader.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a real inner product space and $g : E \to E$ any map; write $u$, $\Delta = 1 - \|x\|^2 + \langle x, u\rangle^2$, $t = -\langle x, u\rangle + \sqrt{\Delta}$ and $f(x) = x + tu$ as above, and let $\Omega = \{x : x \ne g(x),\ \Delta(x) > 0\}$. Then $\|f(x)\| = 1$ for every $x \in \Omega$; if $x \in \Omega$ with $\|x\| = 1$ and $\|g(x)\| \le 1$ then $f(x) = x$; $f$ is smooth on $\Omega$ whenever $g$ is smooth, and $\Omega$ is open whenever $g$ is continuous. Finally, if $g$ carries the closed unit ball into itself and has no fixed point there, the whole ball lies in $\Omega$.

chips: $g$ need not map the disk to itself
diff: The formal statements hold in any real inner product space, with no finite-dimensionality, for an arbitrary $g : E \to E$, and on the whole open set $\Omega$ where the formulas make sense.
Positivity of the radicand, which Milnor asserts, is the separate claim that the ball lies in $\Omega$: there $\Delta \le 0$ forces $\|x\| = 1$ and $\langle x, g(x)\rangle = 1$, hence $g(x) = x$.
That $f$ fixes the sphere needs only $\|x\| = 1$ and $\|g(x)\| \le 1$, through Cauchy–Schwarz; smoothness of $f$ needs $g$ smooth, and openness of $\Omega$ only $g$ continuous.

items.title: Lemmas 5 and 6 for the disk: a smooth fixed point

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 6
milnor.statement: Any smooth map $g : \mathbb D^n \to \mathbb D^n$ has a fixed point. It follows from Lemma 5 (p. 13), that a compact manifold with boundary admits no smooth map to its boundary leaving the boundary pointwise fixed: a fixed-point-free $g$ would produce the retraction $f$, contradicting the special case that the identity of $S^{n-1}$ extends to no smooth map $\mathbb D^n \to S^{n-1}$.
milnor.note: Lemma 5 is proved, following Hirsch, by choosing a regular value $y \in \partial X$ of $f$: then $f^{-1}(y)$ is a compact $1$-manifold with the single boundary point $y$, while such a manifold has an even number of boundary points.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space with closed unit ball $\mathbb D$. Every $g : E \to E$ that is smooth on all of $E$ and carries $\mathbb D$ into itself has a fixed point in $\mathbb D$. The proof is Milnor's: the retraction of V2.9, extended over $E$ by a smooth cutoff that is the identity on $\mathbb D$ and takes values in a slightly larger ball still inside $\Omega$, and corestricted to the sphere by V2.8, has a regular value $y$ by Brown's corollary; the transversality condition of V2.6 holds at $y$ because the retraction fixes the sphere; so by V2.6 the level set over $y$ inside $\mathbb D$ is a compact $1$-manifold whose only boundary point is $y$.

diff: Milnor's Lemma 5 holds for any compact manifold with boundary; only the case of the disk is formalized, inside this proof, and nothing in the book needs more.
Milnor's $g$ is smooth on $\mathbb D^n$, which for him means smooth on a neighbourhood; the formal $g$ is assumed smooth on all of $E$, and V2.11 shows that nothing is lost for the book.
The retraction is extended over $E$ by a smooth cutoff so that no manifold with boundary is ever a domain, and it is regarded as a map into the sphere through V2.8.
$\mathbb R^n$ is replaced by a finite-dimensional real inner product space, and the degenerate case $\dim E = 0$ is disposed of separately, the ball being then a single point.

items.title: Brouwer's fixed point theorem

milnor.label: §2, Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem
milnor.statement: Any continuous function $G : \mathbb D^n \to \mathbb D^n$ has a fixed point. The theorem is reduced to Lemma 6 by approximation: if $\|G(x) - x\|$ has minimum $\mu > 0$ on $\mathbb D^n$, the Weierstrass theorem supplies a polynomial map $P_1$ with $\|P_1 - G\| < \varepsilon$ there, and $P = P_1/(1 + \varepsilon)$ is a smooth self-map of $\mathbb D^n$ whose fixed point contradicts the minimum once $\varepsilon$ is small.
milnor.note: He points out that this pattern, proving a statement about continuous maps by approximating them with smooth ones, recurs later (§8, Problem 4).

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space with closed unit ball $\mathbb D$. Every $G : E \to E$ that is continuous on $\mathbb D$ and carries $\mathbb D$ into itself has a fixed point in $\mathbb D$. The proof is Milnor's, with $\varepsilon = \mu/2$ and the rescaling by $c = 1 + \mu/2$, except that $P_1$ is smooth rather than polynomial: each coordinate $\langle b_i, G\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis is approximated within $\varepsilon/(N+1)$ by Stone–Weierstrass applied to the subalgebra of continuous functions on $\mathbb D$ that extend to smooth functions on $E$.

diff: Milnor's $G$ is a map $\mathbb D^n \to \mathbb D^n$; the formal $G$ is defined on $E$ and assumed only to be continuous on $\mathbb D$ and to carry it into itself, which is the same statement.
$\mathbb R^n$ is replaced by a finite-dimensional real inner product space, of which $\mathbb R^n$ is the case in the book.
The polynomial approximation from the Weierstrass theorem is replaced by an approximation by maps smooth on all of $E$; the final estimate and the rescaling by $1 + \mu/2$ are Milnor's.

items.title: Lemma 2, second clause: the normal space

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 2
milnor.statement: The second sentence of Lemma 2: for a regular value $y$ of $f : M \to N$ and $M' = f^{-1}(y)$, once the null space of $df_x$ is known to be the tangent space $TM'_x$, it follows that $df_x$ maps the orthogonal complement of $TM'_x$ in $TM_x$ isomorphically onto $TN_y$. Milnor states it in one clause and leaves the dimension count to the reader. "Orthogonal complement" needs no comment from him: his manifolds are subsets of $\mathbb R^k$, so every tangent space is a linear subspace of a Euclidean space and comes with its inner product.
milnor.note: The first clause is V2.3, and in the book the two are one lemma with one two-line proof.

lean.statement: In the situation of V2.2 and V2.3 — $M$ and $N$ smooth manifolds without boundary over boundaryless models with corners, $f$ of class $C^\infty$, $y$ a regular value, and the model spaces satisfying $\dim Z + \dim F = \dim E$ — write $T \subseteq E$ for the tangent space of $f^{-1}(y)$ at $p$, realised inside the model space $E \cong T_pM$ as the range of the derivative of the inclusion. Then $df_p$ is injective on the orthogonal complement $T^\perp$; every vector of $TN_y$ is $df_p(v)$ for some $v \in T^\perp$; and the two halves are bundled into a continuous linear isomorphism $T^\perp \to TN_y$ whose underlying map is $df_p$ itself. The model space $E$ of the source carries an inner product, in which $T^\perp$ is taken; the target needs none.

chips: inner product on the source's model
diff: The one hypothesis Milnor does not state is an inner product on the model space $E$ of the source, in place of the bare norm of V2.2 and V2.3. He has it for nothing, his manifolds being subsets of $\mathbb R^k$; the target $N$ needs none.

"The orthogonal complement of $TM'_x$ in $TM_x$" becomes the orthogonal complement of the subspace $T \subseteq E$ of V2.3, the range of the derivative of the inclusion read in the model space, because the tangent spaces of $M$ and of $f^{-1}(y)$ are modelled on different spaces.

The dimension count is written out: at a regular value $df_p$ is onto, so $T = \ker df_p$ has dimension $\dim E - \dim F$ and $\dim T^\perp = \dim F$; injectivity on $T^\perp$ is the first clause together with $T \cap T^\perp = 0$, and surjectivity follows because an injective map between spaces of equal finite dimension is onto.
Injectivity and surjectivity are also available separately and elementwise, which is the form the proofs use; Milnor asserts only the isomorphism.

items.title: Lemma 4 for the cylinder's two ends

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 4
milnor.statement: Take a smooth $f : X \to N$ from an $m$-manifold with boundary to an $n$-manifold, $m > n$, and let $y$ be regular for $f$ and also for what $f$ does on $\partial X$. Then $f^{-1}(y)$, sitting in $X$, is a smooth $(m-n)$-manifold whose boundary is what $\partial X$ cuts out of it, namely $f^{-1}(y) \cap \partial X$. In §4 this is used on the cylinder $X = M \times [0,1]$.
milnor.note: He states it for an abstract manifold with boundary and leaves to a footnote on p. 20 the fact that $M \times [0,1]$ is one, bounded by two copies of $M$.

lean.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds without boundary, $f : M \to N$ smooth, $y$ a regular value, and let $Z$, $Z'$ be finite-dimensional with $\dim Z + \dim N = \dim M$ and $\dim Z' + 1 = \dim Z$. Let $g_0, g_1 : M \to \mathbb R$ be smooth, and suppose that at each point of $f^{-1}(y)$ where $g_i$ vanishes some tangent vector is killed by $df$ but not by $dg_i$, and that $g_0$ and $g_1$ never vanish at the same point of $f^{-1}(y)$. Then, inside the manifold $f^{-1}(y)$, the set $\{g_0 \ge 0,\ g_1 \ge 0\}$ is a manifold with boundary $\{g_0 = 0\} \cup \{g_1 = 0\}$. No compactness is assumed.

diff: Milnor's $X$ is any manifold with boundary; the formal one is $\{g_0 \ge 0\} \cap \{g_1 \ge 0\}$ inside a boundaryless $M$, with $g_0, g_1$ never zero together on $f^{-1}(y)$.
Regularity of $y$ for $f|\partial X$ becomes a transversality condition: at each zero of $g_i$ on $f^{-1}(y)$ some vector is killed by $df$ but not by $dg_i$.
The dimension hypotheses $\dim Z + \dim N = \dim M$ and $\dim Z' + 1 = \dim Z$ carry Milnor's $m > n$; the cylinder is the case $g_0 = t$, $g_1 = 1 - t$ on $M \times \mathbb R$.
Because being a manifold with boundary is local, the two ends are handled one at a time and glued, which is why disjointness of the zero sets is enough.

items.title: Regularity at the ends of the cylinder

milnor.label: §4, p. 21
milnor.statement: The book has no statement here. In the proof of the Homotopy Lemma Milnor asserts at once that $F^{-1}(y)$ is a compact $1$-manifold whose boundary is $f^{-1}(y) \times \{0\} \cup g^{-1}(y) \times \{1\}$. The hypothesis of Lemma 4 that $y$ be regular for $F$ restricted to $\partial(M \times [0,1])$, which is where regularity for the two end maps is used, is never checked.
milnor.note: It is a step inside a proof rather than a statement, and the book does not isolate it.

lean.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be manifolds without boundary of the same dimension, $M$ modelled on $E$, and let $F : M \times \mathbb R \to N$ be smooth. If $y$ is a regular value of $F$ and of the end map $F(\cdot, c)$, then at each $(x, c)$ with $F(x, c) = y$ there is a vector $v = (v_1, v_2) \in E \times \mathbb R$ with $dF_{(x,c)}v = 0$ and $v_2 \ne 0$. This is precisely the transversality hypothesis of V4.1 for $g_0 = t$ at $c = 0$ and for $g_1 = 1 - t$ at $c = 1$.

chips: step of a proof, not a statement
diff: Nothing in the book corresponds to this: it is the unstated verification that Lemma 4 may be applied to the cylinder, isolated here as a lemma.
Equality of dimensions is what makes it work: the kernel of $dF_{(x,c)}$ is nontrivial by counting, and meets $T_xM \times 0$ only in $0$ because $d(F(\cdot,c))_x$ is injective.
The formal statement assumes $y$ regular for $F$, but the proof appeals only to regularity of the end map $F(\cdot, c)$; that hypothesis is never used.

items.title: The Homotopy Lemma

milnor.label: §4, Homotopy Lemma
milnor.statement: Take two maps $f, g : M \to N$ that are smoothly homotopic, the two manifolds having equal dimension and $M$ being compact with empty boundary. Then at any $y \in N$ that is regular for each of them, the counts $\#f^{-1}(y)$ and $\#g^{-1}(y)$ have the same parity.
milnor.note: A smooth homotopy for him is a smooth map on $M \times [0,1]$, a manifold with boundary two copies of $M$ by the footnote on p. 20.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a compact, Hausdorff, second countable smooth manifold without boundary and $N$ a Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary of the same dimension. Let $F : M \times \mathbb R \to N$ be smooth, $f = F(\cdot, 0)$, $g = F(\cdot, 1)$. If $y$ is a regular value of $f$ and of $g$, then $\#f^{-1}(y) + \#g^{-1}(y)$ is even.

diff: A smooth homotopy is taken to be a smooth map on $M \times \mathbb R$, not on $M \times [0,1]$, so its domain has no boundary and Lemma 4 and Brown's theorem apply to it directly.
Milnor's homotopies extend to this form after reparametrizing $t$, and the level set is cut down to $M \times [0,1]$ by hand, so the two notions of smoothly homotopic agree.
$M$ is assumed Hausdorff and second countable and $N$ Hausdorff; second countability is used only for Brown's theorem applied to $F$ on the noncompact $M \times \mathbb R$.
The conclusion is the evenness of $\#f^{-1}(y) + \#g^{-1}(y)$ rather than a congruence; both fibres are finite by compactness and regularity.

items.title: The Homogeneity Lemma

milnor.label: §4, Homogeneity Lemma
milnor.statement: Given any two points $y$, $z$ in the interior of a smooth connected manifold $N$, some diffeomorphism $h$ of $N$ takes $y$ to $z$ and is smoothly isotopic to the identity. Smoothly isotopic in the sense defined on p. 21: joined to the identity by a smooth homotopy on $N \times [0,1]$ every stage of which is again a diffeomorphism.
milnor.note: He proves it by the time-one flow of a compactly supported vector field on a chart ball, remarking that for $N = \mathbb S^n$ a rotation suffices.

lean.statement: Let $N$ be a Hausdorff, preconnected smooth manifold without boundary. For any $y, z \in N$ there are a diffeomorphism $h$ of $N$ with $h(y) = z$ and a smooth map $H : N \times \mathbb R \to N$ with $H(\cdot, 0) = \mathrm{id}$, $H(\cdot, 1) = h$, and every stage $H(\cdot, t)$ a diffeomorphism of $N$.

diff: Milnor allows $N$ to have a boundary and takes $y, z$ in its interior; the formal $N$ is boundaryless, so the restriction to interior points does not arise.
The isotopy is a smooth map on $N \times \mathbb R$ rather than $N \times [0,1]$; that every stage is a diffeomorphism is part of the formal conclusion, as in Milnor's definition.
Hausdorff is assumed on $N$, used once to see that the chart image of a closed ball is closed. Preconnected also allows $N$ empty, which the given $y, z$ exclude.
In the proof the flow of the field $u \mapsto \varphi(u)c$ is replaced by a single Euler step, the explicit map $u \mapsto u + \varphi(u)c$ of the model space, which changes no hypothesis.

items.title: Diffeomorphisms preserve regular values

milnor.label: §4, p. 24
milnor.statement: The book has no statement here. In the proof of the Theorem Milnor writes down, without argument, that $h \circ f$ has $z$ as a regular value and that $(h \circ f)^{-1}(z) = f^{-1}(y)$, where $h$ is the diffeomorphism supplied by the Homogeneity Lemma with $h(y) = z$.
milnor.note: Both facts are used in a single line of the proof, and the second is presented as a computation with $h^{-1}$.

lean.statement: Let $M$, $N$ be manifolds without boundary, $f : M \to N$ smooth, $h$ a diffeomorphism of $N$, and $y$ a regular value of $f$. Then $h(y)$ is a regular value of $h \circ f$, and $(h \circ f)^{-1}(h(y)) = f^{-1}(y)$. The derivative of a diffeomorphism is surjective: the chain rule on $h^{-1} \circ h = \mathrm{id}$ makes it injective, and it is an endomorphism of the model space.

chips: unstated step of the Theorem's proof
diff: The book has no such lemma; both assertions occur inside the proof of the Theorem on p. 24 with no justification offered.
The formal lemma needs only that $M$ and $N$ are boundaryless and $f$ smooth: compactness of $M$, connectedness of $N$ and equality of dimensions play no part.

items.title: Theorem of §4: independence of the value

milnor.label: §4, Theorem
milnor.statement: Under the standing hypotheses of the section — $M$ compact and boundaryless, $N$ connected, the two of equal dimension, $f : M \to N$ smooth — the number of preimages has the same parity at any two regular values $y$, $z$: $\#f^{-1}(y) \equiv \#f^{-1}(z) \pmod 2$.
milnor.note: The Theorem carries no letter and no number; its standing hypotheses on $M$ and $N$ are set out in the sentence just before it.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a compact, Hausdorff, second countable smooth manifold without boundary, $N$ a Hausdorff, preconnected smooth manifold without boundary of the same dimension, and $f : M \to N$ smooth. If $y$ and $z$ are regular values of $f$, then $\#f^{-1}(y) + \#f^{-1}(z)$ is even.

diff: $M$ is assumed Hausdorff and second countable and $N$ Hausdorff; for Milnor's submanifolds of $\mathbb R^k$ these hold automatically and are never mentioned.
Connectedness of $N$ is used in the weaker form of preconnectedness, which also allows $N$ empty, and the conclusion is stated as the evenness of a sum rather than a congruence.
Compactness of $N$ is not assumed, matching Milnor's parenthetical on p. 20 that one may as well assume it but need not.

items.title: The degree modulo 2

milnor.label: §4, p. 24
milnor.statement: Having shown that the residue class is the same at every regular value, Milnor calls it $\deg_2(f)$; the name is announced already on p. 20. He does not say which regular value computes it, because by the Theorem the choice is immaterial and Sard's theorem supplies one.
milnor.note: The case of a map with no regular value never arises for him, since his $N$ is nonempty.

lean.statement: $\deg_2 f \in \mathbb Z/2$ is defined for an arbitrary map $f : M \to N$ as the parity of $\#f^{-1}(y_0)$ for a regular value $y_0$ picked by the axiom of choice, and as $0$ when $f$ has no regular value at all. Under the hypotheses of V4.6 the choice is immaterial: for every regular value $y$ of $f$, $\deg_2 f = \#f^{-1}(y) \bmod 2$.

chips: defined for any $f$, smooth or not
diff: Milnor names a residue class already known to be well defined; the formal definition must produce a value first, so it chooses a regular value and proves independence afterwards.
The definition applies to any map whatever and returns $0$ when there is no regular value; for smooth $f$ on a second countable $M$ that happens only when $N$ is empty.
The count $\#f^{-1}(y)$ is the formal cardinality, which is $0$ on an infinite set; at a regular value the fibre is finite, so this never bites.

items.title: Theorem of §4: homotopy invariance

milnor.label: §4, Theorem
milnor.statement: The second assertion of the same unlettered Theorem: the common residue class $\deg_2(f)$ is unchanged when $f$ is replaced by a smoothly homotopic map. Milnor proves it by picking, with Sard's theorem, a value regular for both maps at once and chaining the congruences.
milnor.note: He draws from it on p. 24 that the identity of a compact boundaryless manifold is not smoothly homotopic to a constant.

lean.statement: For $M$ and $N$ as in V4.6 and any smooth $F : M \times \mathbb R \to N$, $\deg_2 F(\cdot, 0) = \deg_2 F(\cdot, 1)$. The proof takes a value regular for both ends: the regular values of the first form an open set, and those of the second are dense by Brown's theorem, so the two meet. If $N$ is empty, neither end has a regular value and both degrees are $0$.

diff: The homotopy is a smooth map on $M \times \mathbb R$ rather than $M \times [0,1]$, and the two maps compared are named as its ends $F(\cdot, 0)$ and $F(\cdot, 1)$.
$M$ is assumed Hausdorff and second countable and $N$ Hausdorff and preconnected; Milnor's manifolds have these properties by sitting in $\mathbb R^k$.
An empty $N$ is a separate case, forced by the convention of V4.7 that a map with no regular value has degree $0$.

items.title: Nonzero degree forces surjectivity

milnor.label: §4, p. 20
milnor.statement: The book states no such corollary. The nearest thing is the parenthetical aside made while the section is being set up, that nothing is lost by taking $N$ compact and boundaryless, because a degree into any other target is forced to vanish. That aside is this fact applied to a point missed by the compact image of $M$.
milnor.note: The examples he does draw on p. 24 concern the degree of a constant and of the identity, not surjectivity.

lean.statement: For $M$, $N$ and $f$ as in V4.6, if $\deg_2 f \ne 0$ then $f$ is surjective. A point outside the image is vacuously a regular value with empty fibre, so it computes $\deg_2 f = 0$.

diff: No such corollary appears in §4; the closest sentence is the parenthetical on p. 20 that a mod 2 degree into a noncompact $N$ must vanish.
The argument is that a point not in the image is a regular value with empty fibre, so V4.7 computes the degree there as $0$.

items.title: Orientations and the sign of a derivative

milnor.label: §5, Definitions, pp. 26–27
milnor.statement: An orientation of a finite-dimensional real vector space is an equivalence class of ordered bases, two of them equivalent when the change-of-basis determinant is positive; for the zero space an orientation is the symbol $+1$ or $-1$. An oriented manifold carries an orientation of each $T_xM$, and for $m \ge 1$ these must fit together: around every point there is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$ or $\mathbb H^m$ whose derivative carries each chosen orientation to the standard orientation of $\mathbb R^m$. For $f : M \to N$ between oriented $n$-manifolds and $x$ a regular point, $\operatorname{sign} df_x$ is $+1$ or $-1$ according as $df_x$ preserves or reverses orientation.
milnor.note: He admits boundary from the start, so a chart may land in the half space $\mathbb H^m$, and he fixes the standard orientation of $\mathbb R^n$ to have something to compare with.

lean.statement: An orientation of a finite-dimensional $E$ is a ray of nonzero alternating $n$-forms, the class of the determinant form of a positive basis. For a linear $T : E \to F$ and orientations $a$ of $E$, $b$ of $F$, the sign is the sign of the constant $c$ in $\eta \circ T = c\,\omega$ for representatives $\omega$ of $a$ and $\eta$ of $b$; it is $0$ exactly when $T$ is singular, it is multiplicative under composition and equals $1$ for the identity. An orientation of a manifold $M$ modelled on $E$ is a choice of orientation $o_x$ of $E = T_xM$ at each $x$ such that, for every $x$, the derivative at all nearby $y$ of the extended chart at $x$ carries $o_y$ to $o_x$. The sign of $f$ at $x$ is the sign of $df_x$ for $o_x$ and $o_{f(x)}$, and $M \times \mathbb R$ is oriented by declaring a positive basis of $E$ followed by $(0,1)$ positive.

chips: orientation as a ray of top forms
sign defined for every linear map
diff: Milnor's orientation of a space is a class of ordered bases; the formal one is a ray of nonzero alternating $n$-forms, the class of the determinant form of a positive basis.
Milnor asks for charts onto $\mathbb R^m$ or $\mathbb H^m$ carrying the chosen orientations to the standard one; the formal condition compares $o_y$ with $o_x$ through the chart at $x$ alone.
Milnor defines the sign only at a regular point, where it is $\pm 1$; the formal sign is defined for every linear map and is $0$ exactly when the map is singular.
The dimension $n$ is a parameter of the formal definition, so each theorem carries $\dim E = n$ as a hypothesis; there is no oriented atlas and no standard orientation of a model space.

items.title: Local constancy of the sign of the derivative

milnor.label: §5, p. 27
milnor.statement: The book states nothing here. On p. 27 Milnor asserts that $\deg(f;y)$ is a locally constant function of $y$, and in that assertion the local constancy of $\operatorname{sign} df_x$ in $x$ near a regular point is used without comment.

lean.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds without boundary modelled on $E$ and $F$ with $\dim E = \dim F = n$, both oriented, let $f : M \to N$ be smooth and $x_0$ a regular point. Then $\operatorname{sign} df_x = \operatorname{sign} df_{x_0}$ for all $x$ in a neighbourhood of $x_0$. A variant assumes $f$ smooth only on an open set containing $x_0$.

chips: variant for f smooth on an open set
diff: Milnor never states this; it is the step behind his remark that the signed count is locally constant, and its proof is the chain rule in charts with the continuity of a determinant.
The open-set variant, where $f$ is smooth only near $x_0$, is what Lemma 1 needs for the pair maps built from a local coordinate along an arc.

items.title: The signed count deg(f; y) and its local constancy

milnor.label: §5, p. 27
milnor.statement: For $M$ compact and $N$ connected, oriented $n$-manifolds without boundary, and $y$ a regular value of a smooth $f : M \to N$, the degree at $y$ is $\deg(f;y) = \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y)} \operatorname{sign} df_x$. As in §1, this integer is a locally constant function of $y$, and it is defined on a dense open subset of $N$.
milnor.note: He asserts the local constancy in a single sentence, with a reference back to §1 and no proof.

lean.statement: $\deg(f;y)$ is defined at every $y$ as the finite sum of $\operatorname{sign} df_x$ over $f^{-1}(y)$, with the convention that a sum having infinitely many nonzero terms is $0$. If $M$ is compact and Hausdorff, $N$ Hausdorff, $\dim E = \dim F = n$, both oriented and without boundary, $f$ smooth and $y$ a regular value, then $\deg(f;y') = \deg(f;y)$ for every $y'$ near $y$, regular or not. Outside the range of $f$ the count is $0$.

chips: density of regular values not included
