Part a) is formalized in Milnor's case $g = f$, where $y \ne z$ already makes the preimages disjoint; the version for two maps adds the hypothesis that $g^{-1}(y)$ and $f^{-1}(z)$ be disjoint.
Without it one should not expect local constancy, since moving $y$ can push $g^{-1}(y)$ through $f^{-1}(z)$; that is an informal observation, and no counterexample is formalized.

items.title: Problem 15: odd p, compositions, the Hopf map

milnor.label: §8, Problem 15
milnor.statement: If the dimension $p$ is odd then $H(f) = 0$. For a composition $S^{2p-1} \xrightarrow{f} S^p \xrightarrow{g} S^p$, $H(g \circ f)$ is $H(f)$ times the square of the degree of $g$. The Hopf fibration $\pi : S^3 \to S^2$ is given by $\pi(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) = h^{-1}\!\left((x_1 + i x_2)/(x_3 + i x_4)\right)$, where $h$ is the stereographic projection to the complex plane, and Milnor asks for $H(\pi) = 1$.
milnor.note: He specifies $\pi$ only through that formula, and fixes no orientation conventions for $h$, for $S^2$, or for the preimages.

lean.statement: With $p \ge 2$ and all maps smooth: $H(f) = 0$ for odd $p$, and $H(g \circ f) = (\deg g)^2\, H(f)$. The Hopf fibration is formalized as the quadratic map $\pi(z_1, z_2) = (2 z_1 \bar z_2,\ |z_1|^2 - |z_2|^2)$ on $S^3 \subseteq \mathbb C^2$ with $z_1 = x_1 + i x_2$ and $z_2 = x_3 + i x_4$; it equals Milnor's $h^{-1}(z_1/z_2)$ wherever $z_2 \ne 0$, for $h$ the stereographic projection from $(0,0,1)$, every point of $S^2$ is a regular value, and $H(\pi) = -1$. The two fibres used are the great circles over $(1,0,0)$ and $(-1,0,0)$, and the value $-1$ is the product of three signs: both fibre directions are negatively oriented as preimages, and the derivative of the linking map sends them to a negatively oriented basis. The comparison with other sign conventions below is an informal consequence of the formal sign lemmas, not itself a formal theorem.

diff: Milnor asks for $H(\pi) = 1$; with his conventions taken literally the formal value is $-1$, a matter of convention rather than an error in the mathematics.
Those conventions are: $S^k$ oriented as the boundary of the disk, outward normal first; preimages oriented as in §5; $A \times B$ a product; $\lambda(x, y) = (x - y)/\|x - y\|$.

Any one of three equally natural changes restores $+1$: taking $\lambda(x, y) = (y - x)/\|y - x\|$, ordering the product as $B \times A$, or reversing the orientation of the target $S^2$ of $\lambda$.
Reversing the orientation of $S^3$, or of the target $S^2$ of $\pi$, changes nothing, since both preimage orientations reverse at once; the other two parts need only $p \ge 2$ and smoothness.

items.title: Problem 16: transversality

milnor.label: §8, Problem 16
milnor.statement: Two submanifolds $N$ and $N'$ of $M$ intersect transversally if at each $x \in N \cap N'$ the subspaces $TN_x$ and $TN'_x$ together generate $TM_x$; when $n + n' < m$ this means that $N \cap N' = \emptyset$. Milnor asks that a framed submanifold $N$ be deformable slightly so as to meet a given $N'$ transversally, and that the resulting intersection be a smooth manifold.
milnor.note: "Deformed slightly" is left imprecise, and he asks only that the intersection be a manifold, not what its codimension or tangent space is.

lean.statement: As in §7, $M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ is a submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^m$ and $N, N'$ are submanifolds of $M$ of dimensions $n, n'$ and codimensions $p, p'$, with all tangent spaces read inside $\mathbb R^{K+1}$; transversality is $TN_x + TN'_x = TM_x$ at every common point. If $n + n' < m$, transverse submanifolds are disjoint. If $p + p' \le m$, a transverse intersection is a submanifold of $M$ of codimension $p + p'$ whose tangent space at $x$ is $TN_x \cap TN'_x$. For a framed $N$ with a product neighbourhood $G : N \times B_\varepsilon \to M$, which needs $M$ compact and nonempty, and for any $\delta > 0$, there is $u$ with $\|u\| < \delta$ such that $N_u = G(N \times \{u\})$ is a submanifold, $x \mapsto G(x, u)$ is injective and moves no point of $N$ by as much as $\delta$, and $N_u$ meets $N'$ transversally.

chips: codimension p + p′ and tangent space
needs p + p′ ≤ m; M compact nonempty
diff: "Deformed slightly" is made precise: the translate $N_u = G(N \times \{u\})$ inside a product neighbourhood is transverse to $N'$, injectively parametrized, and within any prescribed $\delta$ of $N$.
The intersection is not only a manifold: it is a submanifold of $M$ of codimension $p + p'$ with tangent space $TN_x \cap TN'_x$, stated under the hypothesis $p + p' \le m$.
The deformation goes through the Product Neighborhood Theorem of §7 and so assumes $M$ compact and nonempty; the statements about intersections assume neither.
Transversality is formulated with the tangent spaces read inside the ambient $\mathbb R^{K+1}$, as everywhere in §7, and $M$ itself is a submanifold of Euclidean space.

items.title: Problem 17: the intersection product

milnor.label: §8, Problem 17
milnor.statement: Let $\Pi^p(M)$ be the set of all framed cobordism classes of codimension $p$ in $M$. Milnor asks that the transverse intersection operation be used to define a correspondence $\Pi^p(M) \times \Pi^q(M) \to \Pi^{p+q}(M)$.
milnor.note: He says nothing about how the intersection is to be framed, and does not mention that transverse representatives have to be found first.

lean.statement: $\Pi^p(M)$ is the set of framed cobordism classes of framed submanifolds of the compact nonempty $M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, indexed by the dimension $n$ as well as the codimension $p$ and empty unless $n + p = m$. For transverse framed $F$ of codimension $p$ with framing $v$ and $G$ of codimension $q$ with framing $v'$, with $p + q \le m$, the intersection is framed by $w_k = A^*(AA^*)^{-1} e_k$, where $\alpha_F$ is the linear map sending each $v_i$ to $e_i$ and vanishing on the vectors orthogonal to all the $v_i$, $\alpha_G$ is its counterpart for $v'$, and $A = (\alpha_F, \alpha_G)$ is surjective along the intersection by transversality. For $p \ge 1$ every pair of classes has transverse representatives. For $p, q \ge 1$ with $p + q \le m$ there is a map $\Pi^p(M) \times \Pi^q(M) \to \Pi^{p+q}(M)$ carrying the classes of transverse $F, G$ to the class of the framed intersection, and for $p \ge 1$ it is the only such map.

chips: p, q ≥ 1 and p + q ≤ m
diff: The formal product is built for $p, q \ge 1$ and $p + q \le m$; $p, q \ge 1$ comes from the theorems of §7 that the proof uses, whose arguments rotate regular values, and is not claimed necessary.
Transverse representatives exist, and the product is determined by its values on them, under $p \ge 1$ alone; the book states neither fact.
The framing is written out: $w_k$ is the vector in the span of $v$ and $v'$ for which $(\alpha_F w_k, \alpha_G w_k)$ is the $k$-th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^p \times \mathbb R^q$.
$\Pi^p(M)$ carries the dimension $n$ as a second index and is empty unless $n + p = m$, and $M$ is required to be compact and nonempty, as it already is in §7.

items.title: Problem 17: Πᵖ(M) as an abelian group

milnor.label: §8, Problem 17
milnor.statement: If $p \ge \tfrac12 m + 1$, Milnor asks that the disjoint union operation be used to make $\Pi^p(M)$ into an abelian group, comparing with the corresponding discussion on p. 49.
milnor.note: One line of exercise, with the zero and the inverses left entirely to the reader.

lean.statement: Let $M \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ be compact and nonempty, let $n + p = m$, and let $m + 2 \le 2p$, which is Milnor's condition read over the integers. Then any two classes in $\Pi^p(M)$ have disjoint representatives, and if $F \sim F_1$ and $G \sim G_1$ with $F, G$ disjoint and $F_1, G_1$ disjoint, then $F \sqcup G \sim F_1 \sqcup G_1$, so disjoint union descends to classes. It makes $\Pi^p(M)$ an abelian group whose zero is the class of the empty submanifold and in which $-[F]$ is the class of $F$ with its first framing vector reversed. The formal group structure also takes $p \ge 1$ as a hypothesis, which is redundant, since $m + 2 \le 2p$ implies it.

chips: indexed by n, with n + p = m
diff: $\Pi^p(M)$ is a set of classes indexed by the dimension $n$ as well as by the codimension $p$, and $n + p = m$ is needed for the empty submanifold to count as a framed submanifold at all.
The zero is the class of the empty submanifold and $-[F]$ the class of $F$ with its first framing vector reversed; the book leaves both to the reader.
The formal group structure carries $p \ge 1$ as an extra hypothesis, which is redundant because $m + 2 \le 2p$ already implies it.
Milnor's $p \ge \tfrac12 m + 1$ is written $m + 2 \le 2p$, and $M$ is compact, nonempty and embedded in $\mathbb R^{K+1}$.

notFormalized.title: The index sum is the Euler characteristic
notFormalized.label: §6, pp. 35 and 40
notFormalized.book: Milnor states the Poincaré–Hopf theorem in the form that the index sum equals the Euler number $\chi(M) = \sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{rank} H_i(M)$, and refers to Hopf and to the literature for the identification; p. 40 sketches the three further steps it would take.
notFormalized.instead: **What is proved is the integer, not its name.** V6.9 produces an integer that is the index sum of every smooth tangent field with finitely many zeros on a compact submanifold of Euclidean space, and identifies it with the degree of the Gauss map, which is the form Milnor proves. V6.10 and V6.14 make it computable, as a sum of signs of determinants, and V6.15 computes it for the sphere: it is $1 + (-1)^n$, and it is pinned down, any integer with the Poincaré–Hopf property being that one. **What is missing is the name.** The identification of that integer with the Euler characteristic is not formalized, and the statement cannot even be written down: Mathlib has no Euler characteristic of a topological space, no Betti numbers and no singular or cellular homology with ranks to alternate, so $\chi(S^n) = 1 + (-1)^n$ is not a sentence of the library. Supplying it would mean building a homology theory and computing it for manifolds — the work of a library rather than of a chapter — and Milnor does not prove it either, referring to Hopf's theorem. It is therefore not planned, and it is the one place where this edition is further from the book than a count of lines suggests. Out of reach for a related reason: the Poincaré–Hopf theorem for a manifold not presented as a submanifold of Euclidean space, which would need Whitney's embedding theorem, Milnor working with $N \subseteq \mathbb R^k$ as well.
